# pgedge

> Unified CLI for the pgEdge product suite: `pgedge <module>
> <resource> <verb>`. Supports text, JSON, and YAML output. Designed
> for both human operators and AI agents.

This document ships inside the binary: run `pgedge llms` to print it
from any installed copy — no repo checkout needed. AI agents should
read it before composing commands instead of improvising from
`--help`.

This file is the INDEX. It covers what is true across the whole CLI:
global flags, configuration and profiles, environment variables,
output formats and exit codes. Each top-level command group has a page
of its own, listed under Top-Level Commands.

## Modules

Each module ships its own reference. Print it with `pgedge llms
<module>`, and read only the one you are working in.

| Module | Reference | Covers |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| `starfleet` | `pgedge llms starfleet` | Starfleet: authentication, API clients, invites, memberships, tenant |
| `controlplane` | `pgedge llms controlplane` | A self-hosted pgEdge Control Plane |

`starfleet` splits one level further, because its tree carries two
product sub-trees. Read the sub-reference for the one you are working
in rather than the whole module:

| Sub-reference | Print with | Covers |
|---------------|-----------|--------|
| `starfleet byoc` | `pgedge llms starfleet byoc` | pgEdge BYOC clusters, databases, backups, ingresses, tasks |
| `starfleet managed` | `pgedge llms starfleet managed` | pgEdge Managed single-master databases and their MCP, RAG and PostgREST services |

Each of those is itself an index ending in a Pages table, one page
per resource, read with the command path (`pgedge llms starfleet byoc
cluster`). The `database` page routes once more, to its sub-resources
(`pgedge llms starfleet managed database mcp`). Read the index, then
only the page for the resource you are working on.

The whole `starfleet` tree shares one connection: authenticate once
with `pgedge starfleet auth login` and every starfleet subcommand,
byoc and managed included, borrows it. `controlplane` has no login: it
targets `--base-url` directly, at a Control Plane you run yourself,
which the controlplane reference's "Getting a Control Plane" section
covers.

`byoc` runs databases in your own cloud account, on clusters and nodes
you create. `managed` runs single-master databases pgEdge hosts and
operates, with no cluster or node to choose. The two read alike
deliberately, and the managed sub-reference names where they differ.

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED: pgedge -->
# pgedge

**Usage:** `pgedge <command> [flags]`

Unified CLI for the pgEdge product suite

**Flags:**

| Flag | Required | Default | Description |
|------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `--config string` | No |  | Path to config file (default ~/.pgedge/cli/config.yaml) |
| `--debug` | No |  | Dump HTTP requests and responses to stderr (implies --verbose) |
| `--no-color` | No |  | Disable color in text output |
| `-o, --output string` | No | `text` | Output format: text, json, yaml |
| `--profile string` | No |  | Use a configured profile (see 'pgedge profile list') |
| `-v, --verbose` | No |  | Log requests and responses to stderr, without bodies |

<!-- END GENERATED -->

## Installation

You are reading this from an installed binary, so the CLI is already
installed here. To install it on another machine, hand the install to
an AI agent there: `README.md` in the pgEdge/pgedge-cli repository
opens its Install section with a prompt written for one. This document
is embedded in the binary, so you may be reading it with no checkout —
fetch the prompt without one:

    gh api repos/pgEdge/pgedge-cli/contents/README.md --jq .content \
      | base64 -d

It needs an authenticated `gh` unless the repository is public.

## Shell completion

After installing, enable Tab completion:

```bash
pgedge completion install
```

This installs automatically for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell. Any
shell's script can also be printed on its own with `pgedge completion
<shell>` for manual wiring.

## Global Flags

These persistent flags are registered on the root command and apply
to every module and resource — see the `pgedge` command reference
near the top of this document for the current flag table.

Module-specific flags — for example the starfleet module's `--api-url`,
`--client-id`, and `--client-secret` — are documented in that
module's own reference.

A stray argument to any group command (`pgedge starfleet bogus`,
`pgedge starfleet byoc cluster bogus`) is a usage error (exit 2). That
holds with `--help` appended: `pgedge
controlplane bogus --help` is exit 2 with an `unknown command` message
and no help, so `<cmd> --help` is a reliable test of whether a command
exists. A leaf's own arguments are
a different matter: `pgedge starfleet tenant get --help` prints help
at exit 0 with no ID supplied, because a leaf's arguments are checked
only when it runs.

A near miss offers the correction, at every depth and with `--help`
appended: `pgedge starfleet tenat` names `tenant`.

## Dry Runs

Every verb that writes to an API accepts `--dry-run`. It runs each
client-side check the CLI has, stops before the write leaves the
process, and reports the request that would have been sent: the
actual bytes the generated client assembled.

**Example:**

```bash
pgedge starfleet managed database mcp deploy 3f1c2a9e-5b7d-4e8a-9c6f-0d2b4a8e1f37 \
    --allow-writes --dry-run
```

```text
checks passed:
  ✓ database 3f1c2a9e-5b7d-4e8a-9c6f-0d2b4a8e1f37 resolved
  ✓ no "mcp" service already deployed (deploy intent)
would send:
  PATCH https://api.pgedge.com/managed/v1/databases/3f1c2a9e-5b7d-4e8a-9c6f-0d2b4a8e1f37
  {
    "services": [
      {
        "mcp_config": {
          "allow_writes": true
        },
        "service_type": "mcp"
      }
    ]
  }
nothing was written; the server was not consulted and may still reject this request.
```

What a dry run proves, and where it stops:

- Requests that only READ still go to the API, so `--dry-run` needs
  working credentials and a reachable API. `deploy` and `update`
  fetch the resource first to tell each other apart.
- This is a CLIENT dry run, as in kubectl's `--dry-run=client`.
  Neither Starfleet nor Control Plane has a validate endpoint, so a
  clean dry run means every check this CLI can perform passed, not
  that the API accepted anything. Under `-o json` and `-o yaml` the
  report carries `server_validated: false`.
- The previewed body is masked and bounded exactly as `--debug` output
  is (see Diagnostics), so a large spec's preview is truncated.
- "Writes" is decided per OPERATION, not per HTTP method. Control Plane
  declares two state-changing operations as `GET` (`cluster init` and
  `task cancel`), and a dry run stops those exactly as it stops a POST.
- The exit codes a dry run produces are the real run's: a clean dry run
  is 0, a bad flag is 2, an unknown resource is 4, a plan-entitlement
  rejection from a read is 5. It cannot produce a code only the server
  would have reached, so **`cmd --dry-run && cmd` is not a gate on the
  real run's exit code**. Treat a clean dry run as "the checks listed
  passed", and read the list.
- Which checks a verb has is a property of that verb, and the report
  lists the ones it ran. A check that measures a flag against a list
  the CLI fetches costs a read, so the same bad value can answer 2 or
  5 depending on whether credentials are configured. The byoc and
  managed references name their checks, including what is NOT checked;
  for `controlplane` and `starfleet`, read the report.
- When a check refuses the command, the checks that had already passed
  print to stderr before the error, as text even under `-o json`.

`--dry-run` is registered only on verbs that write. On a read-only verb
it is an unknown flag (exit 2). `--dry-run` and `--dry-run=checks` are
the same thing, and `checks` is the only accepted value;
`--dry-run=server` is rejected with a message naming the missing
platform capability.

Six commands change only local state (the config file, the token cache
or a shell rc file) and have no `--dry-run`: `pgedge profile use`,
`pgedge controlplane config set`, `pgedge starfleet auth login`,
`pgedge starfleet auth logout`, `pgedge completion install` and
`pgedge completion uninstall`. `pgedge controlplane database init`
has none either: it sends no request.

## Configuration and Profiles

Configuration lives at `~/.pgedge/cli/config.yaml`. It holds named
profiles, each carrying per-module sections — for example a
`starfleet` section with an API URL and credentials, written by
`pgedge starfleet auth login`. Select a profile with `--profile` or
`current_profile` in the config file; the built-in default profile is
named `default`.

A profile name must name a profile that already exists. Anything else
fails with exit 1 and a message naming the profiles that do exist, or
how to create one when none do. The rule covers the `--profile` flag,
`current_profile`, `pgedge profile show <name>` and `pgedge profile use
<name>`, so a hand-edited `current_profile` naming nothing is rejected
rather than silently resolving to the default production URL.

The built-in `default` is accepted without a matching section by the
first three, even with no config file at all. `pgedge profile use
default` fails on a config with no `default` section: to return to
the built-in, remove the `current_profile` line.

Two commands create the profile they name, and so accept a name with
no matching profile: `pgedge starfleet auth login --profile
<new-name>` and `pgedge controlplane config set --profile <new-name>`.

**Six commands are exempt from the unknown-profile rule**: `version`, `llms`,
`help` and the whole `completion` tree never read the config, and the two above
create the profile. All six still fail the checks below.

`--config` names the file the profiles live in. A missing path, or
one naming a directory, is exit 1, and an empty value is exit 2. Only
the default `~/.pgedge/cli/config.yaml` may be absent, because a first
run has none yet: to use a new path, create the file and its directory
first.

An EMPTY `--profile` is exit 2: `--profile "$P"` with the variable
unset would otherwise resolve `current_profile`, and a profile is a
tenant, so the silent answer is a different account. Omit the flag to
ask for the active profile.

Both `--config` checks and the empty `--profile` check run before the
command, so `--help` and completion requests (`__complete`) still
exit 0.

Two commands keep working when `current_profile` itself is the
unresolvable one, because they are the way out: `pgedge profile list`
marks the active row `yes (unresolved)` with no Starfleet URL
(`"resolved": false` under `-o json`), and `pgedge profile use <name>`
writes a good name back. An explicitly typed `--profile <unknown>` is
still rejected on both.

Commands that write the config edit it in place: comments, key order,
indentation and keys this version does not recognize are preserved, so
an older binary can safely write a config a newer one created. Blank
separator lines are dropped, and `starfleet auth logout`
deliberately deletes the stored `client_id` and `client_secret`.
`starfleet auth login` keeps the secret in the OS keychain, not the
file, unless no keychain can be used or `--insecure-storage` is
passed.

## Environment Variables

| Variable | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| `NO_COLOR` | Disables color output |
| `PGEDGE_CLIENT_ID`, `PGEDGE_CLIENT_SECRET` | Starfleet credential, both or neither |

`NO_COLOR` is the only environment variable that affects how output
is rendered. The credential pair ranks between the flags and the
profile, and acts as a separate profile that is never saved: no
credential or API URL comes from the config file, nothing is written
to it, the token cache goes unused, the API URL is `--api-url` or
the production default, and `--profile` alongside it is exit status
2.
`pgedge llms starfleet` has the full rules. No other `PGEDGE_*`
variable is read, so an exported API URL or profile is ignored. (cobra's completion
protocol reads two variables of its own, with `COBRA_*` fallbacks —
`PGEDGE_COMPLETION_DESCRIPTIONS`, which trims suggestion
descriptions when set to a false value, and the currently inert
`PGEDGE_ACTIVE_HELP` — and both touch shell completion only.)

Three variables are read as plumbing, not configuration: `HOME`
locates the config file, the token cache and the completion install
paths; `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is honored only by completion's fish path
(and PowerShell's profile fallback); and `SHELL` drives completion's
shell autodetect and the shell row in `doctor`.

## Exit Codes

One number, one meaning, across every module. This table is the whole
contract.

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | General runtime failure |
| 2 | The command was malformed |
| 3 | Timed out |
| 4 | Not found |
| 5 | Authentication failed |

**2 covers every way of getting the command wrong**: an unknown command or
flag, a missing required flag, a missing or extra positional argument, an
unsupported `--output` value, a `pgedge help` topic that resolves to no command
at any depth (`pgedge help <group> <typo>` is 2, not the group's help), and
`--client-id` without `--client-secret` (or the reverse). Read stderr for
which.

**An input file a command was pointed at counts as part of the
command.** A `-f` spec, a `--pipeline-config` file or a TLS file that
is absent, a directory, unreadable, unparseable or structurally
invalid is exit 2, and no write is sent. The config file is the
exception: it is read on every invocation, so a missing, unreadable or
unparseable one is exit 1 (see Configuration and Profiles).

**5 is the server or the credential store saying no**: no credentials resolve
at all, a rejected client ID or secret, a 401/403 from the API, or a
plan-entitlement 400 (below). `starfleet auth login` and `starfleet auth
status` report it the same way every resource command does. On `controlplane`,
exit 5 is any 401 or 403, and `pgedge llms controlplane` names the paths that
classify a refusal themselves and never exit 5.

**A plan-entitlement 400 is 5, not 1.** Some byoc capabilities are
plan-gated server-side: the API answers a 400 whose body contains
`plan does not allow ...` when the tenant's plan doesn't cover the
resource. The CLI reports that as exit 5, the same class as a rejected
credential. Other list verbs are not plan-gated and answer 200 with an
empty array on any plan: `pgedge llms starfleet byoc` says which is
which.

**A router-level 404 is 1, not 4.** A Starfleet 404 whose body is not a
Starfleet error — the API router's plain `{"message":"Not Found"}`,
a proxy or SSO gateway's HTML page, an empty body, anything missing
the `code` field every pgEdge error carries — means the server does
not serve the endpoint at all: the base URL is not a Starfleet API
root, the server is older than this CLI, or something in front of it
answered instead. The CLI reports "this server does not serve an
endpoint this command needs" and exits 1, while a handler's JSON
not-found error (`{"code":404,...}`) exits 4. The controlplane module
draws the same line against its router's plain "404 page not found".

In every module, a non-JSON error body labeled as JSON is still
classified by its status rather than failing to decode. Response
bodies quoted in an error message are truncated and redacted, but
classification always reads the whole body.

Four deliberate exceptions:

- `pgedge starfleet doctor` exits **0** even when authentication is
  broken, because it is meant to be safe to run when auth is the
  suspected problem. Read `auth.authenticated` in `-o json`, not `$?`.
- `pgedge controlplane doctor` exits **0** for the same reason,
  including when the Control Plane is **unreachable**, has no cluster,
  or the active profile carries a field that will not parse. Read
  `reachable` and `cluster_initialized` in `-o json`, not `$?`.
  <!-- doc-gate: correct-for controlplane cluster_initialized — a key controlplane doctor
  builds into its own json map, not a field of any generated struct --> So `pgedge controlplane doctor && <next step>` is not a gate,
  and `reachable` alone is not readiness either.
- `pgedge controlplane config view` exits **0** on a profile it cannot
  fully resolve, and reports the offending value as a `problem` row.
- `pgedge profile use <unknown>` and `pgedge --profile <unknown>` both
  exit **1**, not 2: the name is well formed and names nothing. The
  flag form is exempt on the six commands Configuration and Profiles
  names.

## Paging

`--limit` and `--offset` mean the same thing wherever a verb has them.
Exactly eleven verbs carry `--limit`: byoc's six list
verbs plus `backup-repository get`, managed's three list verbs, and
`controlplane task list`, which has no `--offset`. On any other verb
an `unknown flag` exit 2 is the flag not existing.

**Omitting a flag is how you ask for the server's default.** A value
it cannot mean is refused locally at exit **2** with **no request
sent**: `--limit 0`, `--limit -1`, and any negative `--offset`.
Writing `--limit "$N"` with `N` unset is the usual way that happens.
`--offset 0` is an ordinary value and is sent.

**Any maximum is per ENDPOINT, not per flag name.** Where the API
publishes a bound the CLI enforces it and the error names it. Where it
publishes none the CLI enforces none, even where the server is known
to clamp. Only managed declares any maximum, on two operations, and
`--offset` has none anywhere.

**A server-side clamp is reported.** Every byoc and managed list verb that
takes `--limit` prints a `Showing first N results...` hint to stderr when a
page comes back full, so `managed task list --limit 500` returning 100 rows
says so. The API reports no total, so the hint means more rows MIGHT exist:
page with `--offset` to find out. `managed database list` applies no default
page, so only a `--limit` you set can cut it short. A full `controlplane task
list` page may be truncated, and `pgedge llms controlplane` says how to narrow
it. A verb without `--limit`, such as `managed size list` or `database service
list`, returns everything. Check a verb's `--help` to see whether it is paged.

## Diagnostics

Two ordered levels, both on **stderr** so `-o json` stays pipeable into
`jq` with either one on. They apply to every module.

`--verbose` logs one line per request and one per response: method, URL,
status, elapsed time, and a masked `Authorization` header when one was
sent.

`--debug` adds every request and response header and both bodies.
**`--debug` implies `--verbose`** — passing it alone gives you the
superset, and passing both is the same as passing `--debug`.

    $ pgedge starfleet byoc cluster get abc --debug
    > GET https://api.pgedge.com/byoc/v1/clusters/abc
    > Authorization: ████
    > Accept: application/json
    < 200 OK (412ms)
    < Content-Type: application/json
    < {"id":"abc","name":"prod","plan_expires_at":null}

`--debug` is the tool for a question about the wire that a typed result
cannot answer, such as whether a field arrived as an explicit `null` or
was omitted, which the parsers collapse to the same Go `nil`.
Bodies are printed as the bytes that arrived, so that distinction
survives.

What it hides:

- Credential-bearing values. `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`,
  `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie` and `X-Api-Key` are masked as `████`. A JSON
  body carrying `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `client_secret` or
  `password` at any depth is replaced by its top-level key names — so
  the token exchange shows its shape and never its secret.
  <!-- doc-gate: deliberately-wrong refresh_token — the redactor watches the whole OAuth2 credential family, not only fields a pgEdge struct declares; no struct declares this one and covering it anyway is the point -->

- More than 8 KB of any one body. It says when it truncated, and gives
  the full byte count.

Answer a wire question with `--debug` rather than `curl`: it shows the
payload without anyone handling a raw credential.

## Output

**A `-o yaml` key is the `-o json` key.** The renderer normalizes every
payload through its json tags before encoding yaml, so a `yq` path
always matches the equivalent `jq` path, and an unset optional field
is absent from both. Generated API types render their json tag
(`has_credentials`, not `hascreds`). `pgedge version` declares yaml
tags identical to its json tags (`build_date`). The map payloads of
`pgedge controlplane doctor` and `pgedge controlplane config view`
keep their keys verbatim, so snake_case survives: `base_urls`,
`server_version`.
<!-- doc-gate: correct-for controlplane server_version — a key of controlplane doctor's
map payload, which is the point being made: it belongs to no struct,
so no struct-field scan can find it -->

**A success carrying no body prints nothing to stdout**, under `-o
json` and `-o yaml` as well as text: most deletes, both modules'
`rotate-password`, `managed database resize`, `byoc backup create`,
`byoc database restore` and `controlplane cluster join`. The
acknowledgment is **exit 0**, and the sentence for a person goes to
stderr, which keeps `<cmd> -o json | jq` clean. The rule follows what
the API returns, not the verb name: `controlplane database delete`,
`controlplane host remove` and both modules' `database service remove`
return an object and print it. Read the spec or `-o json` to tell
which kind a verb is.

`byoc backup-repository get` is the one read that can print nothing at
exit 0, when the repository holds no data for that node. That is no
document, not the `[]` an empty list prints, so test the output for
emptiness before parsing it. `starfleet auth logout` and `controlplane
config set` also exit 0 with nothing on stdout. `--dry-run` is the
exception to all of this: its report is the result, so it goes to
stdout in the requested format.

Read the status, never stdout:

```bash
set -e
pgedge starfleet managed database rotate-password "$DB_ID" --role app --force
```

A failure exits non-zero, so an empty stdout at exit 0 means the
operation succeeded.

## Top-Level Commands

`version` and `llms` are documented here. Each other top-level group
has its own page:

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED: pgedge version -->
## pgedge version

**Usage:** `pgedge version`

Print the pgedge CLI version

<!-- END GENERATED -->

Print the version of the unified pgedge binary and each module it
carries, with the launcher's build commit and date. Honors the global
`-o` flag: text (default), json, or yaml.

**Example:**

```bash
pgedge version
pgedge version -o json
```

Expected (text): line 1 is the bare launcher version (grep-stable),
then `commit:` and `build date:` lines, then a `modules:` block with
one `<name> <version>` line per built-in module. `-o json`/`-o yaml`
add a `modules` array to the version object.

---

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED: pgedge llms -->
## pgedge llms

**Usage:** `pgedge llms [module|page] [sub-reference]`

Print the AI-agent reference

<!-- END GENERATED -->

With no argument, print this index to stdout: global flags,
configuration and profiles, environment variables, exit codes, and
tables routing you to each module's reference and each top-level
command's page. With a module name, print that module's reference
instead; with a module and one of its sub-references, print that
sub-scope alone. With a top-level command group, such as `inspect`,
print that group's page. The documents are embedded in the binary, so they are always
available and always match the installed version — AI agents should
run this before composing commands.

**Example:**

```bash
pgedge llms
pgedge llms starfleet
pgedge llms starfleet byoc
```
